stories.headline: Cousins breaks tie with 2:18 left in the Senators' 4-2 victory over the Mammoth
stories.summary: — Nick Cousins broke a tie on a deflection with 2:18 left and the Ottawa Senators beat the Utah Mammoth 4-2 on Saturday night.
stories.body:
OTTAWA, Ontario -- — Nick Cousins broke a tie on a deflection with 2:18 left and the Ottawa Senators beat the Utah Mammoth 4-2 on Saturday night.


Shane Pinto added an empty-net goal with 16 seconds left.


Fabian Zetterlund and Michael Amadio also scored for the Senators (11-6-1). Samuel Ersson turned away 30 shots for his third victory of the season.


Clayton Keller and Barrett Hayton scored for the Mammoth (10-7-1), with Karel Vejmelka making 17 saves.


The Mammoth played the fifth and final game of a trip where they went 2-2-1.


The Senators took a 2-1 lead at 6:29 of the third on a little give-and-go. Claude Giroux took a pass down low from Amadio and fed it right back for Amadio to score into the open net.


The Mammoth tied it just over three minutes later when Hayton tipped Keller’s shot from just inside the blue line.


Up next
Mammoth: At Vegas on Wednesday night.


Senators: Host Washington on Tuesday night.


------

stories.headline: LA Galaxy miss playoffs again as Real Salt Lake gets final berth
stories.summary: Sergi Solans and Zach Booth scored early and Real Salt Lake clinched a playoff spot while eliminating the LA Galaxy with a 2-1 Decision Day victory over the Galaxy on Saturday.
stories.body:
Sergi Solans and Zach Booth scored early and Real Salt Lake clinched a playoff spot while eliminating the LA Galaxy with a 2-1 Decision Day victory over the Galaxy on Saturday.

Real Salt Lake (13-15-6) snags the ninth and final postseason berth in the Western Conference and will travel to Seattle for a wild-card matchup with the Sounders. The winner will square off against the top-seeded Vancouver Whitecaps in the best-of-three first round.

The Galaxy (11-12-11) have missed the last two postseasons after winning the World Cup in 2024.

Solans and Booth scored three minutes apart to give Real Salt Lake a 2-0 lead in the 13th minute.

Solans used assists from Noel Caliskan and defender Philip Quinton in the 10th minute to score for the 14th time in his first season in the league. Nine of Caliskan's 11 career assists and all three of Quinton's have come this year.

Booth scored unassisted three minutes later for a 2-0 lead. It was the first goal for the 22-year-old rookie midfielder in his 18th appearance and seventh start.

The Galaxy cut it to 2-1 in the 40th minute thanks to an own goal by Real Salt Lake defender Luc de Fougerolles, making his seventh appearance in the league.

Rafael Cabral totaled one save for Real Salt Lake.

JT Marcinkowski saved six shots for Los Angeles.

The Galaxy beat Real Salt Lake 2-1 at home to close out April.

stories.headline: A timeline of how Donald Trump, Dana White forged friendship through the fights
stories.summary: Donald Trump and Dana White's friendship is on display cageside, on political stages and at the White House.
stories.body:
Editor's note: This story has been updated after originally being published in June 2026 before the UFC Freedom 250 event at the White House.

THE 28TH INSTALLMENT of the Ultimate Fighting Championship was a trial run. Though 36 states had banned the UFC, the New Jersey State Athletic Control Board allowed the then-owner, Semaphore Entertainment Group, to host its first sanctioned event on Nov. 17, 2000, at the Taj Mahal in Atlantic City, a hotel and casino owned by real estate mogul Donald Trump.

Fighter Randy Couture returned to the UFC for the first time since 1997 and recaptured his heavyweight championship against Kevin Randleman in the main event, but the most consequential appearance that night happened in the crowd of 5,000 fans.

Dana White attended, not as a UFC official but as the manager of fighter John Lewis. White was with friends Lorenzo Fertitta and Frank Fertitta III, brothers who were Las Vegas casino owners and trained in jiu-jitsu under Lewis. As they soaked in the atmosphere, they discussed all the things they could do when the Fertittas' company, Zuffa LLC, owned an MMA promotion.

Three months later, White returned to Atlantic City as UFC president at Trump's Taj Mahal for UFC 30.

That was a launching pad for the UFC and the beginning of a 25-year friendship between Trump and White that has led to Trump attending numerous UFC events, including four as a sitting president, and White introducing presidential candidate Trump at two Republican National Conventions.

"He is one of my very good friends," White told ESPN before the UFC held a fight card at the White House in June, adding that Trump is one of 10 friends in his small circle. "Like, you have a group of friends in your life that are, especially at my age, you've gone through all the s--- in your life and all this stuff. Me and this guy have been friends for 25 years and ... our relationship gets stronger every year."

On June 14, Trump's 80th birthday, their friendship reached a new landmark when the White House hosted UFC Freedom 250. Presidents have invited championship teams to visit the White House, hosted amateur games on the South Lawn and played tennis or basketball there themselves. But the UFC card was unprecedented -- a live professional sporting event staged on the White House grounds. ESPN combed through archival content from dozens of outlets to present the many ways two careers have crossed, creating a path for UFC fighters to walk into the Octagon on the South Lawn of the White House.

The timeline continues into the fall, with Trump inviting White to join his administration as press secretary.

• Jan. 11, 2001: Zuffa LLC purchases the UFC for $2 million and appoints White as the promotion's president. After having trouble landing a venue to host the UFC's two upcoming events, Zuffa makes a deal with Trump to host UFC 30 and UFC 31 back at the Taj Mahal in Atlantic City.

In all the years since, White has repeatedly expressed appreciation for Trump welcoming his company, saying the casino owner's involvement legitimized the UFC. "None of the venues wanted this," White told CBS's "60 Minutes" in 2025. "They didn't believe in it, they didn't like it, and they were worried about the type of crowd that would show up for this type of event."

After Trump stepped up, White remembered the time this way: "When the Trump brand was here [White holds his hand high overhead] and the UFC brand was down there [holding his hand near the floor], he saw it and said, 'I'd love to have it at my casino.'"

However, Trump's casino business faced severe financial problems at the time. According to PBS's "Frontline," his Atlantic City operation reported a net loss of $133.8 million for the 1999 fiscal year. The umbrella company holding the casinos filed for bankruptcy twice within the following decade.

• Feb. 23, 2001: The first event under Zuffa ownership, UFC 30, is at the Taj Mahal. In the main event, Tito Ortiz successfully defends his light heavyweight championship by slamming Evan Tanner unconscious in 30 seconds. White later said Trump was in attendance all night long at UFC 30 and UFC 31, also at the Taj Mahal, though ESPN could not find visual evidence of it, and the account has been disputed by multiple former UFC employees.

• June 29, 2001: The promotion's next fight card is at 20,000-seat Continental Airlines Arena, the East Rutherford home of the New Jersey Nets and Devils. For the first time, photos and the broadcast show Trump cageside. The UFC then books its next two fight cards in Las Vegas, at Mandalay Bay Events Center and at MGM Grand Garden Arena. White reflected on Trump's early support of the UFC in a 2011 interview, saying, "The guy saw this thing coming, was into it and gave us our first shot, and you'll never hear me say anything bad about Trump."

• Feb. 28, 2003: UFC 41 is held at Atlantic City's Boardwalk Hall, which has nearly three times the seating capacity of the Taj Mahal. Heavyweight Tim Sylvia and lightweight BJ Penn successfully defend their titles. Trump Plaza serves as the corporate host for the event, and the Taj Mahal casino features $5 chips with the UFC headliners' faces on them.

• Oct. 22, 2004: The UFC is back at Boardwalk Hall for UFC 50. It is headlined by Ortiz against a short-notice opponent, but the event is best known for being the card on which Georges St-Pierre first fights for a UFC title. St-Pierre loses to Matt Hughes. Also in the building is a production crew for the soon-to-debut reality TV show "The Ultimate Fighter." When TUF aired months after "The Apprentice" made Trump a reality TV darling, the show launched White to stardom, as well. A USA Today story drew a comparison, saying TUF had cast White in the "Donald Trump role."

• June 5, 2008: Trump calls a news conference at Trump Tower in Manhattan to announce a partnership with a startup MMA promotion, Affliction Entertainment, a venture of the Affliction clothing brand. The new promotion's star is heavyweight Fedor Emelianenko, widely considered the best MMA fighter in the world.

The Affliction brand had a long sponsorship history with the UFC, but when word got out that this new fight promotion was about to launch, the UFC banned its fighters from wearing Affliction clothing. At the introductory news conference, Trump acknowledges the potential competition between the UFC and Affliction by raising a topic that exists to this day in MMA: fighter pay. "If there's only one organization," he says, "you can pay the fighters five dollars and they'll be happy to fight."

However, Trump is not critical of the UFC boss. "I have great respect for Dana White," he says. "Some of the people in the room may not like him. I like him and I think he's done a very good job."

• July 19, 2008: Affliction Entertainment holds its first MMA event at the Honda Center in Anaheim, California, cheekily named "Affliction: Banned." It is headlined by Emelianenko knocking out former UFC heavyweight champion Tim Sylvia in 36 seconds. Two other former UFC heavyweight champs, Andrei Arlovski and Josh Barnett, fight on a card filled with talent signed away from the UFC. Megadeth, interrupting an international tour of summer music festivals, performs during the $39.99 pay-per-view.

Trump is asked afterward whether he thinks Affliction will take over MMA from the UFC. "I think it probably will," he says. "All the fighters want to be with us. I think it probably will take over."

That same night, the UFC holds a hastily scheduled fight card on five weeks' notice, made available on basic cable outlet Spike TV. The main event features a rare non-PPV appearance by the UFC's best fighter, Anderson Silva. White refuses to call this scheduling move counterprogramming, saying simply he is "giving the fans what they want."

• July 24, 2009: Almost exactly a year after its first MMA event, Affliction Entertainment folds. The abrupt end comes after one of the headliners on the promotion's third scheduled fight card, Josh Barnett, fails a steroid screening. Hours after the cancellation of "Affliction: Trilogy," the company announces it no longer will promote fights and instead will return as a clothing sponsor for the UFC.

This development shows White's business vision. At the UFC postfight news conference following Silva's KO win a year earlier, on the same night as Affliction's debut card, White had downplayed Affliction's chances of success, saying, "I figure after tonight those guys will be out of business." Asked why, White added, "Because they spent a lot of money tonight. And I know more about this business than they do. When you spend a lot of money and you don't get that money back, you usually go out of business."

White never mentioned Trump's name in his criticism of Affliction.

• Aug. 18, 2011: The UFC announces a seven-year, $700 million broadcast deal with Fox. White later revealed that Trump sent him a copy of a New York Times writeup about the deal with a note written on it that says, "Congratulations, Dana. I always knew you were gonna do it."

• Nov. 15, 2015: Hours after Holly Holm knocks out Ronda Rousey in a huge upset at UFC 193, Trump posts on X (then known as Twitter): "Glad to see that @RondaRousey lost her championship fight last night. Was soundly beaten - not a nice person!" Months earlier, Rousey had said she was voting for Bernie Sanders and downplayed Trump to CNN: "I don't want a reality TV star to be running my country." Rousey does not respond to Trump's "not a nice person" comment. Years later, she revealed that White asked her in 2016 not to speak badly of Trump. She said she agreed "because I owe Dana my life."

• Dec. 11, 2015: For the first time publicly, White backs Trump's presidential campaign. "Donald will get my vote," White says in an interview with TMZ.

• July 11, 2016: Steven Cheung, the UFC's director of communications and public affairs, leaves the promotion to join Trump's political campaign. Cheung had managed messaging for the UFC and its outspoken CEO since 2013. "When you're in communications, and you have a Dana White-type person, I think he would have learned a lot from that," UFC vice president of regulatory affairs Marc Ratner told NOTUS. "And that may have helped him there with the president."

• July 19, 2016: White speaks at the Republican National Convention in Cleveland, Ohio. The UFC CEO begins his address with, "What's up, GOP? ... I'm sure most of you are wondering, 'What are you doing here?'" He draws applause when he addresses why he supports Trump. "Let me tell you something: I've been in the fight business my whole life; I know fighters," White says. "Ladies and gentlemen, Donald Trump is a fighter, and I know he will fight for this country."

• Nov. 8, 2016: White and his wife, Anne, celebrate their 20th wedding anniversary in New York City and watch election night results from their hotel. When Trump is announced the winner, his son-in-law Jared Kushner calls White to invite him to Trump's victory party at the New York Hilton Midtown. White told reporters that Trump had planned to commemorate his victory at UFC 205 inside Madison Square Garden four days after getting elected. Ultimately, Trump did not attend the fights. "I don't think Donald really realized what his duties were going to be had he won," White said.

• July 11, 2017: At a prefight news conference for an upcoming Floyd Mayweather vs. Conor McGregor boxing match the UFC is promoting, White says the White House had reached out about securing tickets for the president, but ultimately Trump decided not to attend. "[Trump] feels like he'll ruin events," White says. "Secret Service is going to have to go through the place, shut down streets and create crazy traffic."

• Aug. 2, 2018: Trump hosts White and then-UFC fighter Colby Covington at the White House. In the wake of Covington's interim welterweight championship victory over Rafael dos Anjos in June, Covington and White visit the president to celebrate Covington's victory and shoot video for an upcoming UFC documentary.

• Nov. 14, 2018: UFC Fight Pass releases a mini-documentary online called "Combatant in Chief: the Story of Donald Trump's History in Combat Sports" that details White and Trump's long friendship. In a trailer for the film, which has since been removed from the UFC's channels, Trump says, "Well, there is a fighter's mentality -- whether you're in the UFC or whether or not you're president. People like Dana White have that and they have it in spades."

• Nov. 2, 2019: Trump becomes the first sitting U.S. president to attend a UFC event. As he walks out alongside White to cageside at Madison Square Garden in New York for the main card of UFC 244, headlined by Jorge Masvidal vs. Nate Diaz in the first BMF title bout, Trump is greeted by a mix of cheers and boos -- a more favorable reception than earlier in the week when Trump appeared at a World Series game in Washington to a "Lock him up!" chant from the crowd.

At the postfight news conference, White expresses no concern for the mixed reception Trump received. "This is America. You can believe and do whatever you want. If you want to boo, you can boo." he says. "... I just felt like tonight we were gonna walk in and whatever happened happened. The guy told me as a friend he would come see the fights, and he did tonight. I appreciate him, and it was a big night for the sport."

• Feb. 20, 2020: White appears at a Trump rally in Colorado Springs, Colorado, and says he and Trump have gotten closer since Trump was elected president.

• May 9, 2020: Trump congratulates White and the UFC on being the first professional sports league to resume action during the COVID-19 pandemic. "Get the sports leagues back, let's play," Trump says in a video prerecorded outside the White House's Oval Office that airs on ESPN before UFC 249. "Do the social distancing and whatever you have to do, but we need sports. We want our sports back."

• July 10, 2021: Trump attends UFC 264 at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas. This is his first appearance at a UFC event since the end of his first presidential run. Although Trump is in attendance, he is not shown on the broadcast. After the event, White expresses frustration with his production crew. "We were getting ready to show him right between the co-main and main events," White says in an interview with TMZ. "Let me tell you what, massive f--- up by my production team. But, you know, it's live TV and these things happen."

• Dec. 29, 2021: White appears on "The Fight with Teddy Atlas" podcast and recounts his appearance for Trump at the 2016 Republican National Convention. He reveals that his decision to appear was not popular among his associates. "Everybody, and I mean f---ing everybody, told me not to do it," White says. "I'm like, 'Are you crazy, man?' Yeah, there's no f---ing way in hell I'm not doing that for him. Then, once I spoke, you know, our friendship went to a whole 'nother level."

• April 8, 2023: After nearly two years without appearing at a UFC fight card, Trump makes an unannounced appearance at UFC 287 at Kaseya Center in Miami four days after he pleaded not guilty in New York to 34 felony counts of falsifying business records related to a cover-up of an extramarital affair. He walks to his seat flanked by White and another of his friends, musician Kid Rock, whose "American Bad Ass" plays in the arena. As he takes his cageside seat, the crowd stands, cheers and chants "U-S-A." It's the first of six UFC events he will watch in person during his second presidential campaign.

• Nov. 14, 2023: White appears on an episode of Theo Von's "This Past Weekend" podcast. White says he refused to take down a promotional video for Trump from his personal social media accounts after a "big" UFC sponsor asked him to. "Don't ever f---ing call me and tell me who to vote for," he rails.

• June 1, 2024: Two days after he is found guilty in New York on 34 felony counts, Trump is cageside for UFC 302 in Newark, New Jersey. The video of Trump and White walking to the cage while being cheered on by the Prudential Center crowd is used to announce Trump's official TikTok account. "The President is now on TikTok," White says in the video. "It's my honor," Trump responds. Trump gained more than 2 million followers in less than 24 hours after posting the video. To date, his debut post is the second-most-viewed on Trump's TikTok.

At the time, 43% of Americans under age 30 said they got their news from TikTok, according to the Pew Research Center.

• July 13, 2024: There is an assassination attempt on Trump during a presidential campaign rally outside of Butler, Pennsylvania. "I am absolutely sick to my stomach and in complete shock," White posts to social media after receiving the news.

Two days later, White appeared on "The Pat McAfee Show," praising Trump for his resilience during the shooting. "Everybody wants to act like a tough guy, right? Well, when the s--- goes down, you find out who tough guys are and who tough guys are not," White told McAfee. "This guy is the legitimate ultimate American badass of all time. A guy takes a shot at him, he goes down, he stands up and then he starts chanting to the crowd, 'Fight, fight, fight.' I literally was blown away."

• July 18, 2024: White is the final speaker at the Republican National Convention in Milwaukee, tasked with introducing the party's presidential nominee, Trump. His position at the end of the program is notable because the job is usually is reserved for the nominee's spouse or a family member. "The fact that he asked me [to introduce him], and the fact that his family also thought it should be me, is probably one of the greatest honors of all time for me," White later told Time magazine.

• Sept. 10, 2024: During a postfight interview on an episode of "Dana White's Contender Series," White says he spoke to Trump "an hour before" Trump's presidential debate vs. the Democratic nominee Kamala Harris, which Trump said he looked at "like a heavyweight fight."

"First of all, it's the second time he has to debate. He already did a debate," White says, referring to the debate held in the summer between Trump and President Joe Biden. "They didn't like how the debate turned out. They want to kick that guy [Biden] out. He's unfit to run, yet he's still the President of the United States. Now they bring in somebody who wasn't elected to actually be in there."

• Oct. 22, 2024: YouTubers the Nelk Boys post a video with Trump on a private flight. While landing in Las Vegas, Trump calls White to say, "I'm with your favorite people, the Nelk Boys ... I let them ride in the plane, Dana. I don't let too many people ride in the plane, I'll be honest with you" before calling White "the greatest of all time."

• Oct. 27, 2024: White speaks during a Trump rally at Madison Square Garden in New York City, just before election day on Nov. 5. "Ladies and gentlemen, we are nine days away from the most important election of my lifetime," White tells the crowd. "The stakes have never been higher, and the choice has never been clearer."

• Nov. 6, 2024: Hours after Trump is elected president for a second term, White addresses the crowd at an early-morning victory party at the Palm Beach Convention Center in West Palm Beach, Florida, thanking influential podcasters and streamers Adin Ross, Theo Von, the Nelk Boys and UFC commentator Joe Rogan for their part in getting Trump reelected. Each of them platformed Trump ahead of the election.

In an interview with The New Yorker two years later, White said he had been trying to connect Rogan and Trump "for probably like six years." He also said he convinced Rogan to publicly back Trump ahead of the election.

"Early on, I started telling the president, if you stay on Fox, and only Fox, you're going to lose [the election] because most of the people on Fox are already voting for you and every other network says horrible things about you," White told The New Yorker. "You gotta start getting into podcasts."

• Nov. 7, 2024 Sports Business Journal publishes a story in which White says he has no interest serving in President Trump's administration. "Donald Trump is one of my very good friends. He did a great job in his last term as president and I know he will do an even better job the next four years," White tells SBJ. "I have no personal political aspirations."

• Nov. 16, 2024: Trump is back at MSG to take in UFC 309, his first UFC event as president-elect. In the main event, Jon Jones makes his only title defense as heavyweight champion, beating two-time champ Stipe Miocic by third-round TKO. At the postfight news conference, White is asked if Trump's election changes anything for the UFC. "I think it's positive for the world, to be honest with you," he responds. " ... I think for the whole country, it feels like somebody hit the reset button."

White later indicated that this appearance was the first time Trump had mentioned the possibility of an event at the White House. "We were at an event at Madison Square Garden and the president leaned over to me and said, 'You know what? We should do an event at the White House,'" White said. "And I said, 'Yes, yes, we should do an event at the White House.'"

• Nov. 19, 2024: White swears off politics in an interview with The New Yorker, saying, "I'm never f--ing doing this again. ... It's gross. It's disgusting. I want nothing to do with politics."

• Jan. 6, 2025: Mark Zuckerberg, a UFC fan and jiu-jitsu practitioner, appoints White to the Meta board of directors. The Associated Press suggests the move could be partly motivated by a desire to curry favor with the incoming presidential administration.

• Jan. 20, 2025: At Trump's presidential inauguration ceremony, White has a prominent seat among the 600 in the Capitol Rotunda behind presidents Bill Clinton, George W. Bush and Barack Obama.

• April 12, 2025: Trump attends UFC 314 at Kaseya Center in Miami, then UFC 316 at Prudential Center in Newark, New Jersey, two months later.

• July 3, 2025: Trump makes the first public mention of a possible UFC fight card at the White House during a rally in Des Moines, Iowa, to kick off a yearlong celebration of the 250th anniversary of the United States. Trump says he wants upward of 20,000 spectators in attendance on the White House grounds for the fights on July 4, 2026. He also states his intention to host a festival at the National Mall in Washington, D.C., and an athletic competition for high school students from across the country.

"So every one of our national parks, battlefields and historic sites are going to have special events in honor of America 250," Trump says, "And I even think we're going to have a UFC fight."

Despite Trump's announcement, a White House spokesperson says there are no more details to share. White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt later stated that the president was "dead serious."

• Aug. 28, 2025: Two weeks after White teased a trip to Washington to visit with Trump and his daughter Ivanka, the UFC CEO confirms that event planning with the White House is underway.

"We had a meeting at the White House, [which] could not have gone better," White says in a live video on Instagram. "It's gonna be awesome. The White House fight is on. ... I will have more details on that in the next couple of weeks."

• Oct. 5, 2025: Trump says at a celebration of the U.S. Navy's 250th anniversary that the White House fight card will take place on his 80th birthday, June 14. Earlier that week, White claimed it would cost the UFC $700,000 to replace the grass on the South Lawn after the event and that weigh-ins would be held at the Lincoln Memorial.

• Dec. 7, 2025: Trump claims that "eight or nine championship fights" will take place at the White House and that the UFC is not fielding anticipated matchups on other cards in order to book them for June 14. When asked about the matchmaking, White repeatedly says the UFC will not begin arranging White House fights until after the new year.

• March 7, 2026: The UFC announces the White House fight card matchups during UFC 326 at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas. Unlike Trump's prediction, the official announcement features one title fight, an interim title fight and four other bouts.

• April 11, 2026: Trump attends UFC 327 at Kaseya Center in Miami. White recounts in the postfight news conference an exchange he has with Trump, a fan of heavyweight Derrick Lewis, whom he is known to call after wins.

"About an hour ago, the president leans over to me and says, 'Why is Derrick Lewis not on the White House card?"' White recalls. "And I said, 'Hold on, Mr. President.' I stepped away and called Derrick Lewis and said, 'Derrick, the president just asked why you're not on the card. Do you want to fight on the White House card?' He said, 'Of course.'"

During the fight card, Josh Hokit is victorious against Curtis Blaydes in one of the most entertaining heavyweight fights of the year. White says in the news conference that he found Hokit getting into an ambulance after the fight and rewarded him with a matchup against Lewis on the White House card.

• April 25, 2026: Trump attends the White House Correspondents' Association Dinner for the first time as a sitting president and White is "right in front of where the president was," according to the UFC CEO. The president, vice president and their spouses are rushed out of the ballroom after gunshots ring out. White recounts to reporters that guests in the ballroom were instructed to take cover but that he did not obey. Instead, he describes an "awesome" experience.

"Inside, they started up. All of a sudden, it just started getting noisy," White tells reporters. "Tables getting flipped over, guys running in with guns and they were screaming, 'Get down!' I didn't get down -- it was f---ing awesome. I literally took every minute of it in. It was a pretty crazy, unique experience."

• May 6, 2026: Trump hosts UFC fighters on the Freedom 250 fight card in the Oval Office. Lightweight champion Ilia Topuria and his challenger, interim champion Justin Gaethje, are there with Ciryl Gane and Alex Pereira, who will fight for the interim heavyweight title. During the promotional event, Trump shows renderings of the venue on the White House's South Lawn.

"As you know, [on] June 14, we're having a big fight," Trump says. "It's never gonna happen again. It's never happened before."

• May 11, 2026: White writes a letter to Trump, asking him to implore Congress to reverse a provision within the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that places a 90% limit on gambling loss deductions. "The current law makes it irrational to bet in the United States because you could end up owing taxes even when you lose or having a tax bill that exceeds your winnings for the year," White writes. "The UFC supports a healthy, legal sports betting market to drive fan engagement, broadcast value and sponsorships. When legal betting is discouraged, it hurts the ecosystem we've spent years building in partnership with state regulators and licensed operators."

• May 29, 2026: Financial disclosures for Trump's trust fund reveal that it acquired stock in TKO Group Holdings, the parent company of UFC and WWE, on March 25, weeks after White announced the Freedom 250 fights. While the exact figure is unknown, between $15,001 and $50,000 worth of TKO stock is disclosed.

• June 1, 2026: Trump tells Fox News that "you'll never see it again" in reference to the White House hosting Freedom 250 and that he's anticipating high viewership ratings. "Dana is an amazing man," Trump says. "He's done an amazing job, he's put together something that -- this will be the highest-rated event, maybe one of them ever in sports."

• June 14, 2026: After UFC Freedom 250 crowns Justin Gaethje lightweight champion and Ciryl Gane interim heavyweight titlist, Trump lauds the event on social media as "unbelievable" and says it was "one of the most exciting days in the history of our fabled White House."

• Nov. 7, 2026: Trump writes on Truth Social that he has offered the White House press secretary job to White, "a violent Fighter and Warrior." He asks White to bring along several UFC fighters and says, "Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!" CNN, citing a source familiar with the matter, reports that White is not taking the job. White, asked about the job offer during a Zuffa Boxing news conference in London, says he is flying to Washington to meet with Trump on Monday. "I got a lot of jobs already," White says.

stories.headline: NFL Week 9 uniforms: Eagles rock 'Kelly Green,' Chargers don 'Super Chargers'
stories.summary: Here's a look at what each NFL team is wearing in Week 9, led by throwbacks from the Eagles.
stories.body:
While Week 8 meant the debut of two "Rivalries" jerseys, another alternate look returns to the field in Week 9, and a popular throwback comes back.

The Los Angeles Chargers are wearing their "Super Chargers" all-navy threads against the Houston Texans. Unveiled in 2025, the Chargers deemed the navy uniforms "a true modern throwback." It's a nod to threads worn in the 1990s and early 2000s, which coincided with a Super Bowl XXIX appearance and four AFC West titles. The navy jersey includes white modern numbers with an old-school outline and gold trim. The navy pants boast a bolt on the side, while a bolt also runs on the shoulders and helmet. "Super Chargers" is stitched in white on the neckline.

In a trend that's becoming more common around the league, the New York Giants and Philadelphia Eagles offer a matchup of throwback uniforms. The Eagles are rocking their "Kelly Green" threads, while it's a "Vintage White" look for the Giants. "Thursday Night Football" between the Denver Broncos and Seattle Seahawks in Week 6 also brought a throwback threads matchup. Philadelphia brought back the iconic Kelly Green combination in 2023, while New York's look returned in 2025 after a one-year hiatus.

Alternates are still represented well throughout the week, though.

The Baltimore Ravens are wearing their "Purple Rising" combination on "Thursday Night Football" against the Jacksonville Jaguars. Baltimore unveiled the look in the offseason as part of their wardrobe overhaul. It includes a new "Purple Rising" helmet, first introduced in 2024 with the alternate purple jersey. The primary logo appears on the metallic purple lid instead of the front-facing Ravens one. stories.headline: Nuggets beat the Pacers 114-102 in Mexico City behind Nikola Jokic's 19 points
stories.summary: — Nikola Jokic scored 10 of his 19 points in the first quarter and the Denver Nuggets beat the Indiana Pacers 114-102 in Mexico City.
stories.body:
MEXICO CITY -- — Nikola Jokic scored 10 of his 19 points in the first quarter and the Denver Nuggets beat the Indiana Pacers 114-102 in Mexico City.


Jokic also grabbed 13 rebounds and dished out eight assists, while Cameron Johnson added 18 points and Jamal Murray finished with 16 for the Nuggets, who have won four of their last five games.


“I just try to play the game the right way, hopefully we can win more games; to win is the most important thing, I do not think about stats,” Jokic said.


Pascal Siakam scored 23 points and Larry Nance Jr. added 15 off the bench for the Pacers, who were the home team in the NBA’s 35th game played south of the border. Indiana has lost five of its last six games.


The Pacers played without All-Star guard Tyrese Haliburton, who missed the trip due to a hamstring strain.


Denver capitalized on a four-minute Indiana scoring drought in the second quarter with a 15-0 run. Murray's jumper extended the Nuggets’ lead to 64-37 — their largest of the game — with less than a minute remaining in the first half.


“It was tough environment, we are not used to this, the altitude and everything is hard to get going,” Siakam said. “Our force and energy was better in the second half, but it was not enough.”


The Pacers responded in the third quarter, pulling closer following back-to-back 3-pointers from Aaron Nesmith that cut the score to 79-67. A layup by Quenton Jackson with 1:16 left in the quarter further trimmed Denver’s lead to 10.


Jarace Walker hit a 3-pointer that brought Indiana within 102-95 with 7:26 left to play, but the Nuggets answered with six straight points to restore a double-digit lead and secure the win.


The game marked the 35th NBA appearance in the country since the league first brought exhibition games to Mexico in 1992.


No country outside the United States and Canada has hosted more.


Of those 34 previous matchups, 15 were regular-season games, and the last 12 — including Saturday’s tilt between Indiana and Denver — sold out.


“The energy was awesome, I got to admit that there is an atmosphere to this building, when we got out on the court you could feel the juice, and the energy,” said Nuggets coach David Adelman. “The NBA is global and it belongs here too.”


Up next
Nuggets: At Houston on Monday night.

stories.headline: Fernando Alonso was dreaming of top-five finish in rainy São Paulo qualifying
stories.summary: Fernando Alonso said he was briefly dreaming of giving Aston Martin a top-five qualifying finish in Brazil as the rain was at its heaviest on Saturday.
stories.body:
SAO PAULO -- Fernando Alonso said he was briefly dreaming of giving Aston Martin a top-five qualifying finish in Brazil as the rain was at its heaviest on Saturday.

Alonso was given a chance to show his talent when the Interlagos circuit was hit by a heavy rainstorm, weather which always levels out discrepancies in car performance.

The two-time world champion progressed through Q1 and Q2 when the rain was at its heaviest, taking Aston Martin into Q3 for the first time this year.

He was ninth by the end of Q3, which took place on intermediate wet tyres as the rain eased up.

"I think P6 is 1.8 seconds in front of me," Alonso said after the session. "So, yeah, it's way too much in front to really dream about any higher position."

Asked if he felt a big result was possible when the rain was at its most intense, he said: "I was thinking maybe, it depends on the rain intensity, but I was thinking maybe top five was possible."

He admitted he did not get the best out of either Q3 run but did not think a clean lap would have made much difference.

"The tyres had no grip in lap one," he said. "So, I said, 'OK, I will push in lap two.' In lap two, because the energy modes, they already spent a lot of energy on the lap one. I didn't have the full energy in lap two. So, at the end, I ended up in no man's land.

"So lap one was not optimised for the tyres, lap two not for the engine. And I think it was maybe half a second or eight tenths on performance to unlock in Q3. But when I saw the times now, that will only offer me one position.

"I think the top six guys were in an unreachable planet today."

- Lando Norris storms to wet pole in São Paulo in heavily disrupted session

- George Russell fumes at 'wrong decision' from Mercedes after missing out on pole

- Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton Ferrari tensions a 'closed chapter'

Rain is forecast for much of Sunday -- the race begins at 2 p.m. local time.

Alonso expects a challenging race either way but said the rain will make it a more competitive afternoon.

"If it rains, yes, maybe a little bit higher chance," he added. "I think it's going to be very difficult. Fast cars start behind. But, yeah, between the low visibility and the tricky race, always wet conditions will offer us a bit better chance to score points.

"I think in dry conditions, there is no way. We were, I think, P18 this morning in FP3. So, we are struggling a little bit more than expected here. Maybe wet conditions will help us."

stories.headline: Witness: Clase 'inside' pitch info dried up amid Mizuhara case fallout
stories.summary: A witness said that the inside info he used to bet on Clase pitches dried up due to increased scrutiny from the scandal involving Shohei Ohtani's interpreter.
stories.body:
NEW YORK -- A government witness testified Friday in the federal trial of Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz that the inside information he used to bet regularly on Clase pitches in 2023 dried up the next season due to increased scrutiny from the gambling scandal involving Shohei Ohtani's interpreter at the time.

Luis de Aza Baez said he placed dozens of bets and won thousands of dollars by wagering on the velocity of select Clase pitches during the 2023 season, "because I had inside information." Clase is accused of conspiring with bettors to rig 18 pitches over three seasons.

De Aza Baez said that when he asked for more information on Clase pitches in 2024, he was told that because of "what was going on with Ohtani, there was no more information like that."

Ohtani, the Los Angeles Dodgers' superstar, came under scrutiny in March 2024 after ESPN reported that millions of dollars had been sent from his bank account to an illegal bookmaking operation. His longtime interpreter, Ippei Mizuhara, later pleaded guilty to stealing nearly $17 million from Ohtani to pay off gambling debts and is currently in prison. Ohtani was cleared of any wrongdoing.

De Aza Baez, who worked as an Uber driver, told prosecutors that he began receiving information about the pitches from Enoc Pena, an associate of Clase's, in 2023. De Aza Baez said the tips often came through a group chat titled "Uber Inc." that Pena started and included other men who have been referenced in the case and also worked for the ride-share company in Massachusetts at the time.

Prosecutors showed a screenshot of a text message Clase allegedly sent to Pena on Sept. 30, 2023, when the Guardians were scheduled to play the Detroit Tigers, that talked about "killing the first two chickens." De Aza Baez said the message was instructions to bet on a Clase pitch to the third batter of an inning, but only if Clase had retired the first two batters. Clase did not appear in the game.

Clase's defense has argued that mentions of roosters and chickens in such communications often were referencing cockfighting, a legal activity in the Dominican Republic, where Clase and others in the case are from.

De Aza Baez said he became friends with Pena as well as Robinson Vásquez Germosen and Luis Arismendy Paca Méndez, who are co-defendants in the case, while they were all living in Nantucket, Massachusetts. Paca Méndez, who has pleaded not guilty, is not participating in the trial after being extradited from the Dominican Republic to the U.S. on Oct. 19.

De Aza Baez said he met Clase when Vásquez and Pena brought the pitcher to his house for a birthday party on April 28, 2023, in Winthrop, Massachusetts, where De Aza Baez had moved. He met Clase again a few days later at a relative's house. Prosecutors showed a video of the gathering, with Clase playing dominoes on a table featuring a Boston Red Sox logo. The Guardians were in town for a series against the Red Sox.

De Aza Baez said he never received any information directly from Clase, only from Pena. De Aza Baez said he did not have an agreement with Pena but gave him money because he "almost always" won using the information to bet on Clase's pitches. De Aza Baez acknowledged opening a DraftKings betting account under his wife's name to increase the amount he could wager and win on his Clase bets. De Aza Baez also said he included the Clase pitch bets in parlays to maximize payouts.

De Aza Baez acknowledged that he had agreed with the government to forfeit $69,000 from his winning bets on Clase and would "tell the truth" in exchange for prosecutors dropping a wire fraud charge related to the case.

Clase, Ortiz and Vásquez have pleaded not guilty to conspiracy charges of wire and honest services fraud, sports bribery and money laundering.

"Our defense is the same today as it was in opening: This is a case about big talk and small bets," Vásquez's attorney Todd Spodek told ESPN after Friday's hearing. "We're confident leaving that judgment to the jury."

The trial will continue next Thursday in Brooklyn.

stories.headline: Wings' Paige Bueckers, Azzi Fudd talk relationship on pod
stories.summary: Azzi Fudd hosted Wings teammate Paige Bueckers on her podcast and the two discussed their relationship, Dallas' season and Fudd's recovery from knee surgery.
stories.body:
Dallas Wings teammates Azzi Fudd and Paige Bueckers, the past two WNBA No. 1 draft picks, spoke on Fudd's podcast Friday about a variety of topics, including a personal life update.

"We're not together anymore; it's been a while," Bueckers said on the "Fudd Around and Find Out" podcast. "[We] share that because everybody [was] like, 'Oh my gosh, they're teammates, how is this going to work?'"

Bueckers and Fudd, who were teammates in college at UConn, said they felt the need to address their relationship status in part because of allegations it factored into the Wings picking Fudd at No. 1 in April. Fudd was chosen over TCU guard Olivia Miles, who went on to be the Rookie of the Year for the Minnesota Lynx. Spain's Awa Fam (Seattle Storm) was taken third, followed by teammates from the 2026 champion UCLA Bruins: Lauren Betts (Washington Mystics), Gabriela Jaquez (Chicago Sky) and Kiki Rice (Toronto Tempo).

Fudd, Fam, Betts and Miles were all No. 1 at different points in ESPN's mock draft in the months before the April draft. Bueckers said her previous relationship with Fudd had no impact on Dallas' decision.

"We were not together before she got drafted," Bueckers said. "She was not drafted because she was my girlfriend. She was drafted because she deserved it. She's an amazing human, an amazing basketball player. And we're still friends, we're still cool.

"We played an entire season together; we're the utmost professionals."

Fudd averaged 13.1 points but was limited to just 30 games after an injury to her right knee led to season-ending arthroscopic surgery in August. She offered an update on her health.

"My offseason's been good," Fudd said. "Lots of rehab, lots of training, lots of on-court workouts, lots of traveling. It's been busy.

"I think there's a lot I can improve on. Especially the iso game; I feel like I'm not too comfortable with that yet. I know I'm capable of doing a little bit more. Watching someone like Paige who is able to create from anywhere ... that's great inspiration for me."

Bueckers averaged 20.9 points, 4.1 rebounds and 5.9 assists, and was named to the All-WNBA second team as Dallas reached the playoffs as the No. 7 seed.

The Wings were eliminated in the first round by the eventual champion Golden State Valkyries. Bueckers said she learned a lot from her first playoff experience and complimented Golden State.

"The Valkyries' defense, I can't explain to you how tough they are," Bueckers said. "They swarm, they send bodies, they trap you, they blitz you, they're so connected. I'm glad I got to have that experience against them to open my eyes to what the playoffs are like -- the physicality, the pressure, the environment.

"And I'm proud of our season. I hated losing; I sat and was pissed about it for like a week. I reached out to [Sue Bird] about it, what was her first playoff experience like. I didn't play as well as I wanted to. But it was my first experience, going against a really good opponent, and I was learning and growing through it all."

Fudd and Bueckers also addressed the Wings' move to the 19,000-seat American Airlines Center in downtown Dallas next season after playing at UT Arlington's College Park Center, which seats over 7,000, since the franchise relocated to Texas in 2016.

"UTA was a vibe; we had a ball, we did our thing there," Bueckers said. "But definitely excited to move into Dallas. New times."

While the change in venue will lead to more eyes on Wings games, the two players said they're hoping for less scrutiny of any on-court behavior.

Both said fans shouldn't read into interactions the two have with each other or their teammates as anything other than normal team behavior. They also said they don't stand for "hate of any kind" or "tearing people down to lift us up."

"We've seen a lot of negativity," Bueckers said. "We've had stuff sent to us, stuff sent to our family, our friends. There's been some crazy things said about us. We still support each other, we're still going to be great friends, we're still going to be great teammates. All the negative things can be put aside, and you don't need to overanalyze everything."

Fudd added with a chuckle, "Also, we don't need messages [from fans] on what the other person's doing. We've addressed everything we need to, and the rest will stay with us."

stories.headline: Does Man United's coach matter? Could Jurgen Klopp reach Premier League glory at Old Trafford?
stories.summary: If Manchester United hired an all-time great like Jurgen Klopp, would they have won the Premier League? Let's find out!
stories.body:
Right around this time every year, you can start to feel it. The air gets a little crisper. The shadows get a little colder. The days get shorter. The tree colors start to pop. You start wearing sweaters. Pumpkins appear in places where they do and do not belong.

Everyone and everything starts to shift, just slightly, in preparation for what's about to happen. The cycles of nature can be fickle and unpredictable, so the date is never exactly the same, and some years come and go without anything at all. But most years, it does.

Our tiny little rituals prime us to anticipate the inevitable, oncoming shift: that moment when Manchester United fire their manager and convince themselves that the new guy is finally going to be the one who fixes everything.

Ruben Amorim lost his job last January. Erik ten Hag was fired two years ago, right before Halloween. Ole Gunnar Solskjaer got the boot just a couple of days before Thanksgiving. And Jose Mourinho was relieved of his duties a little over a week before Christmas.

Now that we've once again entered the season of sacking, Michael Carrick seems like he will inevitably become the latest victim.

Man United are clear of the relegation zone on goal differential alone. If history is any indication, their comeback against AS Roma in the Champions League will end up being meaningless. Before Tuesday's win, Carrick appeared to be on the verge of tears at the end of every match.

This is the 14th season since Manchester United last won the Premier League. And whoever replaces Carrick will be the ninth coach to try to do something that no other United manager since has done: just, simply, meet the expectations at one of the richest sports teams on the planet for more than a single season in a row.

But given how many different coaches have now failed since Sir Alex Ferguson left the club, it makes you wonder: Could anyone have been successful at Manchester United?

What is a great manager worth?

Arsenal won the Premier League last season with 85 points.

If we lived in a world where there were no subs and everyone on the field contributed exactly evenly to their team's success, then all 11 Arsenal players would have contributed about 8 points (7.7, to be slightly more exact) of value last season.

Except, the alternative to each player isn't just zero points. If you removed Bukayo Saka from the lineup, you wouldn't have to play a man down. No, you'd get to put another player out there who would also contribute to winning to some degree.

So, let's look at the relegation-level cutoff. West Ham were relegated with 39 points. Using the same framework, we'd say that all of their players were worth a little over 3.5 points across the season. We could then say that the average Arsenal player provided 5 more points of value than a relegation-level player.

This, of course, isn't exactly how it works: Some players are better than others, some positions are more valuable than others, and almost nobody plays 100% of the minutes. Goalkeeper David Raya played 97.3% of the league minutes last season, and Declan Rice led all outfield Gunners with 90.5% of minutes played.

But it all still gives us a nice benchmark. The best players on the best teams in the world are probably worth around 7 points more than your average relegation-level player. The truly generational superstars? You could probably bump that number up to 10 points if you wanted to.

But what about the manager? Rather than litigating the whole "managers don't matter" conversation for the 1,000th time on this website, we're just going to go with the logic put forth by Liverpool's former director of research, Ian Graham, in his book, "How to Win the Premier League": "[About] the same value as a good player brings. This is in line with manager salaries -- the best managers are paid a similar wage to the best players."

Who, then, was the best manager that Manchester United could've hired at any point over the past 14 seasons?

Most soccer-watchers would agree that there are two potential answers: Pep Guardiola or Jurgen Klopp. And most analyses would agree.

A 2025 study from the Sloan Sports Analytics conference looked at team performances from 2017 through 2024 across Europe's Big Five top leagues. The study awarded or penalized the manager for how much a team's performance level exceeded or undershot expectations based on the talent of the roster. Klopp and Guardiola topped the list -- with a significant gap between themselves and the next tier of coaches.

Given the 114 guilty charges against Manchester City under Guardiola, though, I think we have to go with Klopp. While Guardiola's influence on how the sport is played is undeniable, we now have to look on his Man City tenure skeptically. We know how much they outperformed what we were told they spent, but it would be foolish to blindly accept those numbers and attribute the gap purely to the Guardiola effect.

With Klopp, though, we know that he turned two clubs that were not even the richest clubs in their own leagues into two of the best teams in the world. And we know that he maintained those levels -- at both clubs -- for many seasons in a row. On top of that, both Borussia Dortmund and now Liverpool seem to have gotten worse after he left each job.

The job of the manager, simply, is to make his team better than the talent his club can afford to acquire and then to keep that improvement going even as the roster turns over. At the highest level of the sport, Klopp was better at that than any of his peers.

Could the best manager in the world save Manchester United?

What, then, might've happened if Manchester United somehow managed to hire Jurgen Klopp back in 2013 instead of David Moyes?

There are, of course, all kinds of ripple effects we could tease out -- what it would've done to German soccer, where Liverpool would've ended up, how Mohamed Salah's career would've played out, and on and on.

But I just want to focus on what it would've meant for Manchester United. We know that Liverpool benefitted from hiring Jurgen Klopp. But we also know that Jurgen Klopp benefitted from working for a club that did things like convincing him to sign Mohamed Salah instead of Julian Brandt.

Liverpool's cutting-edge front office didn't turn the club into the best team in the world, and neither did Klopp. No, it was the combo of the two that did it.

We could say similarly about Borussia Dortmund. At the time, Dortmund were one of the leaders in both youth development and identifying young stars. This meant that Klopp got the ideal kinds of talent, energetic youngsters to play his high-pressing style: Robert Lewandowski, Mats Hummels, Marco Reus, and Ilkay Gündogan -- just to name a few.

What we know about Manchester United, broadly, is that the club is an abject disaster. In terms of doing things that increase their chances of winning games, they are pretty much as bad as it gets. Since 2013, United have finished at or higher in the table than their relative Premier League revenue ranking once -- and that was last season.

While we could employ some magical thinking and convince ourselves that the only problem here is that the club can't hire the right coach, that's obviously not true. If it were, it would mean that the club that keeps firing its coaches just so happens to be doing all of the other things right.

No, the failure to find a successful long-term coach is a symptom of all of the other issues that plague the club. They've so badly underperformed their resources for over a decade; we can confidently say there is something deeply wrong with the way Manchester United tries to build its soccer teams.

So, if Klopp were the Man United coach, he wouldn't have fixed all of those problems. No, he would've had to work within that dysfunctional environment. He would've, in other words, ended up with Brandt instead of Salah -- many times over.

But let's sketch out the absolute best-case scenario for this hypothetical. Let's say that United have continued to hire "relegation-quality" managers. And let's say that Klopp's value is equivalent not just to the best player on a title team but to a true, once-in-a-generation superstar.

Neither of those things is true -- United aren't constantly hiring genuinely bad coaches, and Klopp himself would tell you that he's not worth the same as Lionel Messi -- but stretching the effect out to the extreme helps make the point.

Plus, by applying a Messi-like effect every year, we're canceling out some of the other problems with this exercise: not addressing the Manchester City situation, not subtracting points from other teams, not accounting for the increased spending power from an increased performance level, and so on.

If Klopp could've added 10 points to every Manchester United season, here's how things would've changed:

On average, United would've ended up with 76 points per season instead of 66, and their average finishing position would've been 3.8 instead of 5.3.

So, of course: things would be better if Manchester United had employed the best manager of the modern era for the last decade-plus. In this scenario, they would've finished in the top four 10 times, rather than six. Perhaps there would've been a deep Champions League run at a club that reached three finals in four seasons from 2008 to 2011 and hasn't been beyond the quarterfinals since.

But even if we granted Manchester United 13 straight seasons of consistent, transformative, incomparable, once-in-a-generation managerial performance, the team would still find itself right where it sits today: with no Premier League titles since Sir Alex Ferguson left the club.

stories.headline: Ponga stars as NZ book Cup final spot with Tonga win
stories.summary: New Zealand are into their first World Cup final in 13 years after Kalyn Ponga returned from a broken arm to power the Kiwis past Tonga in a 34-10 win.
stories.body:
New Zealand are into their first World Cup final in 13 years after Kalyn Ponga returned from a broken arm to power the Kiwis past Tonga in a 34-10 win.

At a McDonald Jones Stadium dominated by Tongan flags, Ponga marked his comeback from a 23-day absence with a broken arm with an influential performance in Saturday's semi-final.

The Newcastle fullback set up three of the Kiwis' six tries and pulled off one of the try-saving tackles of the tournament as New Zealand advanced to next Sunday's final in Brisbane.

The Kiwis, who also welcomed back hooker Phoenix Crossland following his lengthy suspension, will learn their opponents on Sunday when Australia face Samoa in the other semi-final.

On the other side of the coin, this was a missed opportunity for Tonga who have failed to reach a single final across three-straight tournaments.

Fullback Lehi Hopoate made five errors and the Tongan halves struggled to master the elements, particularly in the second half when they were running into a ferocious wind.

This semi-final exit is likely to mark the last chance for Jason Taumalolo - the architect of rugby league's Pacific revolution - to win a World Cup.

But there remains a chance for New Zealand to become world champions next week after Ponga marked his return with a protective arm guard to send Briton Nikora crashing over after three minutes.

Tonga soon hit back as Jojo Fifita started and finished one of the most breathtaking tries of the tournament.

Catching a bomb five metres off his own line, the Gold Coast winger surged through a gap in the Kiwis' kick chase, linked with Tui Lolohea and Tolu Koula, who burned Joe Tapine and turned the pass back infield for Fifita to score.

Ponga halted Demitric Vaimauga with an incredible last-gasp tackle to slow Tonga's charge, before Fifita muscled over on the left for his second of the night.

Isaiya Katoa couldn't make the conversion and that was as close as Tonga got to victory.

As halftime approached, the Kiwis edged ahead 12-10 courtesy of Dane Gagai and never looked back.

Hopoate was unable to deal with a bouncing ball to the in-goal under pressure from Ponga and Gagai pounced.

But Tonga were unable to go the distance as Casey McLean, Jahrome Hughes, Xavier Willison and Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad moved New Zealand out of sight with second-half tries.

stories.headline: Jack Hughes scores in overtime as Devils rally past Islanders 5-4
stories.summary: — Jack Hughes scored in overtime to lift the New Jersey Devils to a 5-4 victory over the New York Islanders on Saturday.
stories.body:
NEW YORK -- — Jack Hughes scored in overtime to lift the New Jersey Devils to a 5-4 victory over the New York Islanders on Saturday.


Dougie Hamilton, Luke Evangelista, Declan Chisholm and Evan Rodrigues also scored for New Jersey, which extended its winning streak to four games. Jake Allen made 19 saves.


Hughes scored with 3:42 remaining in overtime, keeping the puck on a two-on-one rush before firing a shot past Ilya Sorokin’s blocker.


Anthony Duclair, Matthew Schaefer, Simon Holmstrom and Victor Eklund scored for New York, which lost its third straight game. Sorokin finished with 45 saves and captain Bo Horvat added two assists.


The Devils erased a two-goal deficit in the third period, capped by Hamilton’s power-play goal with 6:18 remaining in regulation. Jack Hughes curled around the net before finding Hamilton in the slot for the tying goal.


Evangelista started the comeback when he pulled New Jersey within a goal at 6:08 of the third period.


The Islanders took a 2-1 lead after the first period. Duclair opened the scoring with less than five minutes remaining, Rodrigues tied it 17 seconds later and Schaefer put New York back ahead with his fifth goal of the season.


Chisholm tied the score at 2 just 4:42 into the second period when Jesper Bratt fired a shot off the end boards that took an awkward bounce around the net, allowing Chisholm to bury the rebound.


Two of Islanders goaltender Ilya Sorokin’s best saves came against Devils captain Nico Hischier. Sorokin denied Hischier on a breakaway in the closing seconds of the second period and stopped a one-timer in the opening minute of the third.


Up next

Colorado (12-15-7) could have secured a spot in the MLS Cup playoffs with a win.

Dallas (16-8-10) clinched the No. 2 seed in the Western Conference and plays seventh-seeded Portland in the best-of-three first round.

Kaick cut back to evade a defender and blasted a shot from the top of the penalty box under the crossbar and inside the right post that made it 2-1.

Joaquín Valiente put away a first-touch shot, off a cross played by Kaick, that made it 1-1 in the 75th minute and Santiago Moreno capped the scoring in the second minute of stoppage time.

Morgan Whittaker scored a goal for the fourth consecutive game for the Rapids. Nico Hansen had seven saves.

Whittaker, on the counter-attack, put away a first-touch shot off a cross from Georgi Minoungou that gave Colorado a 1-0 lead in the 47th minute. Minoungou, who subbed on to begin the second half, has four assists in the past three games.

Up next Colorado: Season completes.

Dallas: Hosts Portland for Game 1.

stories.headline: The Philippine legend who keeps Jonny Parsons going
stories.summary: Philippine hero Lapu-Lapu defeated Ferdinand Magellan at the Battle of Mactan in 1521, and the story carries a personal meaning for Jonny Parsons that he takes with him every time he steps into the Octagon.
stories.body:
More than 500 years after Lapu-Lapu defeated Ferdinand Magellan at the Battle of Mactan, his legacy continues to inspire generations of Filipinos.

For UFC fighter Jonny Parsons, that story carries a personal meaning that he takes with him every time he steps into the Octagon.

Parsons, a Filipino-American whose mother is from Cebu, learned about the legendary warrior only in 2020, well into his mixed martial arts career. But once he discovered Lapu-Lapu's story, he found a connection to the resilience and spirit that have become part of his identity as a fighter.

"I have the warrior spirit," Parsons told ESPN. "My mom is from Cebu, so I have that Lapu-Lapu fighting spirit in me.

"It's definitely about resilience and holding it down for your people."

On April 27, 1521, Lapu-Lapu led native warriors against Magellan's forces at the Battle of Mactan in the Visayan islands of the Philippines. Using their knowledge of the terrain, the defenders overcame the Portuguese explorer's armed expedition and killed Magellan, disrupting Portugal's efforts to establish control over the islands.

Lapu-Lapu's victory remains a defining moment in Philippine history. He is celebrated as a symbol of Filipino resistance, courage and independence.

Parsons will carry that same resolve into his next challenge. The 35-year-old is set to face José Souza in a welterweight bout at UFC Fight Night: Cortes-Acosta vs. Walker.

"It's just a great story about overcoming the odds," Parsons said.

"They won that battle against Magellan, and in [Lapu-Lapu's] lifetime, the Philippines wasn't conquered. It wasn't until years after he was gone that they were conquered.

"I definitely want to say that my fighting spirit comes from that side of the family."

Parsons will have his own odds to overcome against Souza, as the Brazilian stands 6-foot-3 and holds a 10-inch reach advantage over the 5-foot-9 Parsons.

Souza, 24, carries a 9-1 professional record and is 1-0 in the UFC. On the other hand, Parsons owns a 9-3 record, including a 1-0 mark in the UFC.

The Filipino-American is returning from a layoff of 40 months after persistent hip flexor and groin injuries disrupted his training and kept him away from competition.

Still, he believes he has the tools to deal with the physical disadvantage and make a statement in his return.

"I'm no stranger to fighting a taller, longer opponent," he said.

"I think I have all the tools and weapons to defeat this guy [Souza].

"It just means that everyone's going to be able to see the best Jonny Parsons so far. But not the best ever, because I'm still getting better."

The extended break did not mean stepping away from the sport. Parsons, who is also now a mixed martial arts coach, kept training, shifting his focus to building strength, improving his conditioning, and addressing the physical issues that had held him back.

"This whole time that I've been off, I've been training," he told ESPN.

"I've been focusing on my strength and conditioning to help mend injuries and certain problem areas that were giving me issues during training.

"So I would say right now, I'm the healthiest and strongest I've ever been."

The experience also forced Parsons to rethink how he prepares for fights.

Rather than pushing through every session, he learned to treat recovery as seriously as training to develop a more disciplined approach to keeping his body healthy.

"I put a very heavy emphasis on my strength and conditioning training here in Vegas at the Performance Institute," he said.

"I also put much more effort into my recovery. Sometimes recovery, well, actually all the time, recovery is not just laying in bed and resting.

"Recovery is stretching. Recovery is a cold plunge, a sauna and walking. So I've really developed a much smarter training regimen that has allowed me to train at a very high level while avoiding all types of injuries."

Parsons is ready to show what that patience and discipline have produced.

"I'm very calm when I go into fights, and I'm very peaceful. I know I fight the best when I'm at peace. And it's very easy for me now to find that peace."

stories.headline: Hall of Famer Jack Ham hospitalized, in stable condition after medical emergency
stories.summary: Hall of Fame linebacker and Penn State radio analyst Jack Ham experienced a medical emergency Saturday in Seattle and was in stable condition.
stories.body:
Hall of Fame linebacker and Penn State radio analyst Jack Ham was in stable condition after experiencing a medical emergency Saturday in Seattle, Nittany Lions coach Matt Campbell said after his team's 28-25 win over Washington.

Ham, 77, was transported to University of Washington Medical Center, where he was being treated.

Campbell called it a "gut-wrenching day for Penn State football," and said play-by-play announcer Steve Jones, Ham's longtime radio broadcast partner, made a "heroic effort" in assisting Ham.

"If it's not for Steve, what he did, I don't know if we have as good a news as we do right now," said Campbell, who also praised Washington athletic director Pat Chun and the Huskies' staff for helping Ham.

Ham has been the radio analyst for his alma mater since 2000.

Ham was a six-time All-Pro selection with the Pittsburgh Steelers, with whom he won four Super Bowl championships and made eight Pro Bowl appearances. He earned All-America honors at Penn State in 1970.

He entered the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1988 and the College Football Hall of Fame two years later.

The Johnstown, Pennsylvania, native was named to the NFL's 1970s All-Decade Team and all-time teams for both the NFL and Steelers, who have Ham in their hall of honor.
